stem: A previously healthy young adult suddenly develops sharp unilateral pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath without preceding trauma. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.C: An uncomplicated chest-wall strain with no respiratory involvement.
options.D: Myocardial infarction diagnosed solely from age and chest pain.

rationale: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax commonly presents with sudden sharp pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath in an otherwise healthy person without trauma. Physical findings may include decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance. Therefore A is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize the typical presentation of primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
source_version_date: StatPearls 2026 edition; chapter last updated February 15, 2023
source_locator: History and Physical — primary spontaneous pneumothorax: pleuritic sharp chest pain and shortness of breath
source_claim_supported: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax can cause sudden sharp pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea without trauma; decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance may occur.
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation — acute respiratory disorders and emergency recognition
correction_summary: Removed family-member cueing and the unsupported implication that age alone rules out cardiac disease. Made the item direct pattern recognition and reduced difficulty from hard to easy.
audit_findings: NCBI directly supports A. The final stem specifies no trauma and the typical acute pleuritic/dyspnea pattern. Independent second pass confirmed A is uniquely best.
